units.title: Holdout, cross-validation and resampling by the right unit
outcomes: Choose \(K\)-fold, stratified, group or time-series resampling from the deployment dependence structure and name the sampling unit.
Run nested selection so the reported score never guided the choice it evaluates.
Keep preprocessing inside the resampling loop so no test information leaks into fitting.
units.why: A validation score that guided model choice is optimistic. The sampling unit decides what the error bars mean at deployment.

next.note: Put paired uncertainty on the resampled estimates.
Match the split design to the same dependence structure.

study.locator: Sections 3.1.1 (cross_validate versus cross_val_score, the Data transformation with held-out data note, 3.1.1.2 cross_val_predict and its warning) and 3.1.2 (K-fold, Stratified K-fold, Group K-fold, TimeSeriesSplit)

study.title: Nested versus non-nested cross-validation on iris
study.locator: Whole example: inner GridSearchCV over \(C\) and \(\gamma\), outer cross_val_score; the non-nested best_score_ is optimistic next to the nested mean

study.title: ISLP Chapter 5 lab: validation-set, LOOCV and k-fold errors
study.locator: The Validation Set Approach (linear/quadratic/cubic MSE triple 23.62, 18.76, 18.80 on Auto) and Cross-Validation (LOOCV MSE 24.23, then the 10-fold KFold comparison)
study.depth: Skim the bootstrap half. It belongs to the uncertainty unit.

focus: An integer cv in cross_val_score means StratifiedKFold when the estimator is a classifier and y is binary or multiclass, and plain KFold otherwise, unshuffled in both cases.
cross_val_predict returns one out-of-fold prediction per row for inspection and stacking, but its pooled score is not a generalization estimate.
GroupKFold keeps whole groups out of training together; TimeSeriesSplit only ever tests on the future. The deployment unit picks the splitter.
Every fitted transform (scaling, imputation, selection) must sit inside a Pipeline under CV, or test statistics shape the training features.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the nested loop for an RBF SVC over \(C \in \{1, 10, 100\}\) and \(\gamma \in \{0.01, 0.1\}\) on iris, with KFold(4, shuffle=True) inner (random_state=0) and outer (random_state=1) splits, and state which number is honest. Reference run: nested mean 0.9468 against non-nested best_score_ 0.9603. One trial is noisy: the docs example averages 30 trials and finds a mean gap of only 0.0076 (std 0.0078).
traps: Reporting GridSearchCV.best_score_ as model performance. It was maximized over the same folds, so the nested mean is the honest estimate.
Splitting rows when the deployment unit is a group or a time block. Shared patients, users or days across train and test inflate the score.
Fitting the scaler or selector on all data before cross_val_score. Wrap it in a Pipeline so each fold fits transforms on its train split only.

selfTest.q: When does an integer cv in cross_val_score stratify?
selfTest.a: When the estimator is a classifier and y is binary or multiclass, it uses StratifiedKFold; otherwise plain KFold. Neither shuffles unless asked.

selfTest.q: You select \(C\) by CV and report the best CV score. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: Selection consumed the same scores, so the maximum is optimistic. Re-estimate with an outer loop (nested CV) or a sealed held-out set.

selfTest.q: Each patient contributes several rows. Why is plain KFold wrong, and what replaces it?
selfTest.a: Rows from one patient land on both sides and leak identity. Split by patient with GroupKFold or LeaveOneGroupOut.

selfTest.q: Why must scaling sit inside the CV loop?
selfTest.a: A scaler fit on all data lets test statistics shape training features. Each fold must fit the transform on its train split only.

units.title: Regression error and confusion-matrix metrics
outcomes: Derive MAE, RMSE, R2 and MAPE from residuals and state which error each one punishes.
Reconstruct precision, recall, F1 and support from a confusion matrix and choose macro, micro or weighted averaging deliberately.
Match the regression loss to the decision cost, including quantile (pinball) and relative-error losses.
units.why: Accuracy and RMSE hide the errors that cost money. The matrix and the averaging rule decide what a single number means.

next.note: Compare models across thresholds with ranking and proper scores.
Act on the matrix with cost-derived thresholds.

study.title: Classification metrics: confusion matrix, report, precision and recall
study.locator: Sections 3.4.4.6 (confusion matrix rows are true classes, ravel order tn fp fn tp, normalize modes), 3.4.4.7 (classification report with support) and 3.4.4.9 (precision, recall, F measures and averaging rules)
study.depth: Skip top-\(k\) accuracy, kappa, Hamming and Jaccard unless your problem needs them.

study.title: Regression metrics including decision-weighted losses
study.locator: Sections 3.4.6.1 (R2, including the constant-mean 0.0 and negative cases), 3.4.6.2 and 3.4.6.3 (MAE, MSE, with RMSE via root_mean_squared_error), 3.4.6.5 (MAPE) and 3.4.6.10 (pinball loss)
study.depth: Skim Poisson, Gamma and Tweedie deviances. Read them fully only for count or skewed-positive targets.

focus: Rows of confusion_matrix are true classes; ravel gives tn, fp, fn, tp in that order.
R2 is 1 minus residual over total variance: 0.0 for the mean predictor, negative for worse-than-mean predictions.
Macro averages classes equally, weighted averages by support, micro pools the counts. On imbalance they disagree, and the choice encodes costs.
Pinball loss at quantile \(\tau\) prices over- and under-prediction asymmetrically; MAPE divides by the target, so near-zero targets dominate it.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive F1 as the harmonic mean of precision and recall and R2 as 1 minus \(SS_{\text{res}}\) over \(SS_{\text{tot}}\). Compute F1 on y_true [0,0,0,1,1,1,1,1] with y_pred [0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1]: tn, fp, fn, tp is 2, 1, 2, 3, so precision is 0.75, recall is 0.6 and F1 is 0.667. Compute R2 on the guide's regression example, y_true [3, -0.5, 2, 7] with y_pred [2.5, 0.0, 2, 8]: 0.949.
traps: Reading accuracy on an 80/20 split. The constant classifier scores 0.80, so report balanced accuracy or the full matrix.

Averaging F1 with the wrong rule. Weighted averaging lets the majority class hide a failing rare class, and micro pools the counts so the rare class barely registers; macro gives it full weight. Name the rule.
Comparing RMSE across targets with different units or scales. It carries the target unit, so normalize before comparing.

selfTest.q: tn, fp, fn, tp is 2, 1, 2, 3. What are precision, recall and F1?
When is R2 negative, and what does that say?
selfTest.a: When \(SS_{\text{res}}\) exceeds \(SS_{\text{tot}}\): the predictions are worse than the constant mean of the scored targets. On held-out data that can happen honestly, through overfitting or shift; in-sample, least squares with an intercept cannot go below 0.

selfTest.q: Why can macro-F1 and weighted-F1 rank two models differently?
selfTest.a: Macro weights classes equally so a rare class counts fully; weighted weights by support so the majority dominates. They encode different costs.

selfTest.q: Your target spans cents to millions. Why is RMSE alone a poor objective?
selfTest.a: Squared errors on the largest targets dominate it. A relative loss such as MAPE, a quantile loss, or modeling log amounts matches the decision better.

practice.name: scikit-learn worked examples: confusion matrix and classification report
practice.locator: Reproduce the 3.4.4.6 ravel example (2, 1, 2, 3) and the 3.4.4.7 report (accuracy 0.60, macro average F1 0.49) by hand, then match with code

units.title: ROC AUC, average precision, log loss and Brier score
outcomes: Derive ROC AUC as the pairwise ranking probability and average precision as the precision-recall summary.
Explain why ROC AUC is prevalence-independent while average precision moves with the base rate.
Compute log loss and Brier score by hand and state what each one punishes beyond ranking.
units.why: Ranking scores compare models across thresholds, but only proper scores judge the probabilities you will later threshold, weight or abstain on.

next.note: Repair the probabilities that ranking scores cannot judge.
Turn scores into decisions at a cost-derived threshold.

study.title: ROC, precision-recall, log loss and Brier score
study.locator: Sections 3.4.4.15.1 (binary ROC with predict_proba[:, 1] or decision_function; breast-cancer AUC 0.99), 3.4.4.9 (average_precision_score and precision_recall_curve), 3.4.4.12 (log loss) and 3.4.4.18 (Brier score, binary range and calibration note)
study.depth: Skip multilabel ranking metrics (3.4.5) and DET curves unless your task needs them.

focus: Pass the positive-class column predict_proba(X)[:, 1] (classes_[1]) or decision_function to roc_auc_score, never hard predictions.
The docs' 0.99 breast-cancer AUC is a demonstration, not a result: the snippet re-scores its own training data.
Average precision summarizes the PR curve and falls with prevalence; ROC AUC conditions within each class and does not move.
Log loss punishes one confident error without bound; Brier stays bounded and mixes calibration with discrimination.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute ROC AUC by pairwise comparison on y [0,0,1,1] with scores [0.1,0.4,0.35,0.8] to get 0.75 (3 of 4 positive-negative pairs ordered), plus log loss 0.47 and Brier 0.16, and list the ROC points (0,0), (0,0.5), (0.5,0.5), (0.5,1), (1,1).
traps: Feeding predict() labels into roc_auc_score. Hard labels give one elbow and a collapsed AUC; pass scores.
Quoting the in-sample 0.99 AUC from the docs snippet as model quality. It re-scores training data.
Treating ROC AUC as a calibration check. A model can rank perfectly while its probabilities are badly miscalibrated.

selfTest.q: What does AUC 0.75 mean as a pairwise statement on the reproduce example?
selfTest.a: A random positive outranks a random negative with probability 0.75. Three of the four pairs are correctly ordered; only 0.35 versus 0.4 is flipped.

selfTest.q: Prevalence drops 10x at fixed score distributions. What happens to ROC AUC and to average precision?
selfTest.a: ROC AUC is unchanged because it conditions within each class. Precision at fixed recall falls, so average precision drops.

selfTest.q: Why does log loss explode on one confident error while Brier stays bounded?
selfTest.a: Log loss takes minus \(\log\) of the true-class probability, unbounded as it goes to 0. Binary Brier is the squared error of the positive-class probability, at most 1 per item (the guide's halved form of the two-class sum).

selfTest.q: roc_curve returns thresholds starting at inf. Why is inf not an operating threshold?
selfTest.a: The first point predicts nothing positive (FPR and TPR both 0). Inf sits above every score; the usable thresholds are the distinct scores.

practice.name: Hand-check ROC, AUC and Brier against sklearn
practice.locator: Match your hand computation on y [0,0,1,1] with scores [0.1,0.4,0.35,0.8] (AUC 0.75, AP 0.833) against roc_auc_score, average_precision_score and brier_score_loss, then reproduce the confusion_matrix_at_thresholds table (tns [2,1,1,0], tps [1,1,2,2])
practice.note: All three numbers were verified with sklearn 1.9. Recompute AP by hand from the PR points before checking.

units.stopWhen: Your hand AUC, AP, log loss and Brier match sklearn to 3 decimals, and you can say which metric moves when prevalence shifts.

fit.note: ROC, PR, log loss and Brier all sit in the sklearn metrics page at derive and measure depth.

units.title: Calibration curves and Platt or isotonic recalibration
outcomes: Read a reliability curve bin by bin and summarize it with ECE without letting one number hide the shape.
Fit Platt (sigmoid) and isotonic recalibration on held-out predictions and explain their slope, intercept and monotonicity behavior.
Keep a final test split untouched through fitting, calibration and threshold choice.
units.why: Thresholds, costs and abstention all read probabilities. An uncalibrated 0.9 is a rumor, not a measurement.

next.note: Spend calibrated probabilities on thresholds and reject rules.
Put uncertainty on the calibration comparison.

study.title: Probability calibration: curves and the calibrator
study.locator: Sections 1.16.1 (reliability diagrams via CalibrationDisplay and calibration_curve) and 1.16.2 to 1.16.3 (CalibratedClassifierCV: ensemble averaging versus a single refit, disjoint calibration data)
study.depth: Skip the multiclass example unless your task has more than two classes.

study.title: Sigmoid, isotonic and temperature scaling
study.locator: Sections 1.16.3.1 (Platt sigmoid: logistic slope and intercept, preserves ranking and AUC), 1.16.3.2 (isotonic: free monotonic steps, stronger past about 1000 points, ties can change AUC) and 1.16.3.4 (temperature scaling)

focus: Calibrate on predictions the classifier did not train on: CV inside CalibratedClassifierCV, or a disjoint calibration split with FrozenEstimator.

In sklearn 1.9, cv=None means 5-fold, stratified when y is binary or multiclass, and ensemble='auto' means an averaging ensemble of per-fold pairs unless the estimator is a FrozenEstimator. Posts written before 1.6 show ensemble=True as the default.
Sigmoid fits a logistic slope and intercept: safe on small samples. Isotonic fits a free step function: stronger on large calibration sets, but flat steps tie scores and can move AUC.
Lower Brier or log loss does not prove better calibration. Both mix calibration with discrimination, so read the curve.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, simulate overconfident scores: default_rng(1), n = 4000, p uniform on [0.05, 0.95], y drawn as Bernoulli(p), score s = clip(0.5 + 2.2 (p - 0.5), 0.01, 0.99). Fit a one-feature logistic (Platt) map on the first 2000 rows and score the last 2000: Brier falls from 0.2130 to 0.1892 (slope 2.80, intercept -1.46 on the raw score). Bin the held-out half with sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve at 5 bins: the top bin predicts 0.964 while 0.776 are positive.
traps: Calibrating on training predictions. Outputs pushed to 0/1 teach the calibrator the wrong map; use CV or a disjoint split.
Judging calibration by ECE alone. One number averages away the shape; the user guide warns that lower Brier need not mean better calibrated.
Fitting isotonic on a few hundred points and shipping it. It overfits small calibration sets, so prefer sigmoid there.

selfTest.q: A bin has mean predicted probability 0.8 with 10 of 40 positives, out of 200 items total. What is its ECE contribution?
selfTest.a: The gap |0.8 - 0.25| = 0.55 weighted by the bin share 40/200 = 0.2, so 0.11.

selfTest.q: Why does isotonic recalibration risk changing AUC while Platt cannot?
selfTest.a: Isotonic is stepwise: distinct scores can land on one flat step as ties, which changes ranking. Sigmoid is strictly increasing, so pairwise order survives.

selfTest.q: What goes wrong if you tune the threshold on the calibration split and report on it too?
selfTest.a: The threshold overfits that split's noise. Tune on validation or calibration data, then report once on the untouched test split.

selfTest.q: GaussianNB probabilities pile near 0 and 1. Sigmoid or isotonic, and on what data?
selfTest.a: With ample held-out data, isotonic corrects the characteristic S-distortion better; with little data use sigmoid. Never fit either on the training predictions.

practice.name: Deep-ML 260: Calculate Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
practice.locator: Implement expected_calibration_error and pass both public tests ([0,1] with [0.0,1.0] gives 0.0; four 0.8-probability items with two positives give 0.3)
practice.note: Use equal-width bins, put \(p = 1.0\) in the last bin, skip empty bins and weight by bin share. Then apply the same function to your Platt experiment above.

units.stopWhen: Your reliability table, ECE function and Platt versus isotonic comparison reproduce on held-out data, and the final test split is still sealed.

fit.note: Curves, both recalibrators and the held-out discipline sit in the sklearn calibration page; Deep-ML 260 is the section's single platform exercise.

units.title: Cost-sensitive thresholds, imbalance and prevalence change
outcomes: Derive the cost-optimal threshold \(t = C_{\text{FP}} / (C_{\text{FP}} + C_{\text{FN}})\) for calibrated probabilities and set it with FixedThresholdClassifier.
Tune a threshold with TunedThresholdClassifierCV without letting the tuning data leak into the report.
Specify a selective (reject-option) rule with a coverage target and report its risk-coverage tradeoff.
Predict how a prevalence shift moves precision, F1 and the operating threshold while ROC AUC stands still.
units.why: The default 0.5 threshold encodes equal costs that no deployment has. Imbalance and prevalence change move every thresholded metric except the ranking.

next.note: Test whether the thresholded gap is real or noise.
Find where the thresholded errors concentrate.

study.title: Tuning the decision threshold for class prediction
study.locator: Sections 3.3 (0.5 and score-0 defaults), 3.3.1.1 (TunedThresholdClassifierCV, default balanced-accuracy scoring, pos_label via make_scorer), 3.3.1.2 (internal 5-fold CV; cv='prefit' only on fresh validation data) and 3.3.1.4 (FixedThresholdClassifier with FrozenEstimator)
study.depth: Run the 3.3.1.1 snippet. The page prints 0.88 for the refit model scored on its own training data (0.887 with scikit-learn 1.9.1), against an internal cross-validated best_score_ of 0.86. The gap is in-sample optimism, so trust the 0.86.

study.title: Selective classifier, coverage and selective risk
study.locator: Abstract and Section 2, Preliminary Definitions (Definitions 1 and 2: coverage and selective risk, the risk-coverage tradeoff)
study.depth: Stop before the noise-free learning bounds. The definitions plus your own confidence threshold are the whole assignment.

study.title: Precision and recall definitions for the prevalence arithmetic
study.locator: Section 3.4.4.9 for the binary precision and recall definitions; the prevalence-shift rescaling is derived in Reproduce below

focus: Predict positive when \(p\) times \(C_{\text{FN}}\) exceeds \((1-p)\) times \(C_{\text{FP}}\), so \(t = C_{\text{FP}} / (C_{\text{FP}} + C_{\text{FN}})\). With miss cost 10 and false-alarm cost 1, the threshold is 1/11 = 0.091, not 0.5.

TunedThresholdClassifierCV moves only the threshold by internal CV. When the vanilla model was fit on the same data with the same seed, predict_proba, and so the ROC and PR curves, are identical before and after.
The reject rule is a second threshold: abstain when \(\max(p, 1-p)\) is below 1 minus reject-cost over error-cost, then report risk at the achieved coverage.

At fixed class-conditional score distributions, a prevalence shift moves precision and F1 but not recall, FPR or ROC AUC. The cost-optimal cutoff on the old scores moves too, because the calibrated probabilities change with the base rate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(t = C_{\text{FP}} / (C_{\text{FP}} + C_{\text{FN}})\) and apply it at 10:1 costs (threshold 0.091). Then build make_classification(n_samples=4000, weights=[0.9, 0.1], class_sep=0.8, random_state=0), split 75/25 stratified with random_state=0, fit LogisticRegression on train and wrap it in FixedThresholdClassifier(FrozenEstimator(model), threshold=t). On the 1000 test rows (105 positives) recall rises from 0.238 at 0.5 to 0.714 at 0.2 and 0.848 at 1/11, while precision falls from 0.581 to 0.446 and 0.302.
traps: Tuning the threshold on the test set, or with cv='prefit' on training data. The user guide warns explicitly that tuning data must be disjoint from training data.
Moving the threshold to fix calibration. Thresholds spend probabilities; they cannot repair them. Recalibrate first.
Reporting selective accuracy without coverage. Accuracy on the retained 60% says nothing beside accuracy on 100%; always pair risk with coverage.

selfTest.q: Miss cost 10, false-alarm cost 1, calibrated \(p = 0.2\). Predict positive or not, and why?
selfTest.a: Predict positive: the expected miss cost 0.2 times 10 = 2 exceeds the false-alarm cost 0.8 times 1 = 0.8. Equivalently, 0.2 exceeds 1/11.

selfTest.q: Why do the tuned and vanilla classifiers share ROC curves?
selfTest.a: Tuning moves only the decision threshold while predict_proba is untouched, so every threshold sweep (ROC, PR) is identical.

selfTest.q: Reject cost 0.2, error cost 1. When do you abstain?
selfTest.a: When \(\max(p, 1-p)\) is below 0.8: the cheapest guess has error probability above the price of abstaining.

selfTest.q: Prevalence halves at fixed score quality. Which metrics move?
selfTest.a: Precision and F1 fall; recall, FPR and ROC AUC hold. Any threshold tuned for the old base rate must be re-derived.

practice.name: scikit-learn cost-sensitive threshold example: German credit
practice.locator: Cost-sensitive learning with constant gains and costs: a bad credit scored as good costs 5 times the reverse. Rebuild the vanilla and tuned HistGradientBoosting models, confirm their predict_proba outputs are identical while their labels differ, and read best_threshold_ (0.03 on the page). Then run the cv="prefit" variant (0.25) and the page's explanation of why it overfits

With scikit-learn 1.9.1 the test gain is -209 at 0.5, -143 tuned and -136 at 1/6. Explain why the tuned cutoff sits so far below 1/6.

units.stopWhen: You derive the cost threshold from scratch, reproduce the tuned-versus-vanilla probability agreement, and report a reject rule as a (risk, coverage) pair.

fit.note: Cost-sensitive thresholds sit in the sklearn route; selective prediction failed coverage there, so one verified paper (El-Yaniv and Wiener, Section 2) was adopted.

units.title: Paired bootstrap, permutation tests and multiplicity
outcomes: Report a paired bootstrap interval for a model difference with the resampling unit matched to the comparison.
Run a paired permutation test with the correct permutation type and state its null in words.
Report an effect size beside every p-value and adjust for multiplicity with the search history on record.
units.why: Two models sharing a test set produce correlated scores. Unpaired uncertainty is wider than honest, and unadjusted selection is optimistic.

next.note: Fold the paired interval into the ablation runner.
Localize the significant gap to slices.

study.title: The Bootstrap and paired-sample permutation tests
study.locator: The notebooks linked from this page: Tutorial 3 (The Bootstrap: scipy.stats.bootstrap with paired=True, BCa and percentile intervals, standard errors) and Tutorial 2b (Paired-Sample Permutation Tests: permutation_test with permutation_type='samples')
study.depth: Stay inside Tutorials 2b and 3. The independent-sample and Monte Carlo tutorials solve different comparisons.

study.title: ISLP Chapter 5 lab: the bootstrap standard error
study.locator: The Bootstrap (Portfolio \(\alpha\) standard error 0.0912 via boot_SE with B=1000 and seed 0, then the linear-regression coefficient SEs)

study.title: ISLP Chapter 13 lab: FWER, FDR and the double-dip
study.locator: Family-Wise Error Rate (Bonferroni rejects only Manager One; Holm rejects Managers One and Three at FWER 0.05; the best-versus-worst paired test at \(p = 0.038\) rises to 0.186 under Tukey's method) and False Discovery Rate (Benjamini-Hochberg on all 2,000 managers)

focus: Resample pairs, not models: one index stream (paired=True) must score both models, or shared example difficulty becomes noise.
The paired-difference test is permutation_type='samples' (sign flips within pairs). 'pairings' tests association instead; 'independent' shuffles labels across groups.

Pairing shrinks intervals. In the reproduce simulation a 4.8-point gap on 500 items has a paired 95% interval about 0.038 wide, against about 0.120 when each model is resampled on its own, which then covers zero.
Every tuned, selected or re-run comparison spends error budget. Record the search history and report Holm (FWER) or BH (FDR) adjustments beside raw p-values and effect sizes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement a paired bootstrap for an accuracy difference (one index stream for both models, 9999 resamples, percentile interval) plus a paired permutation test. Simulate shared difficulty: default_rng(0), \(u\) uniform on 500 items, model \(A\) right when \(u < 0.70\) and model \(B\) when \(u < 0.65\), so \(B\)'s hits are a subset of \(A\)'s, the strongest pairing. Accuracies are 0.662 and 0.614; expect a paired interval near [0.030, 0.068] against near [-0.010, 0.110] when each model is resampled independently.
traps: Bootstrapping each model's scores with its own rng stream. Unpaired resampling destroys the pairing and inflates the interval.
Using permutation_type='pairings' (or 'independent') for a paired model comparison. That tests correlation (or cross-group exchangeability), not the mean paired difference.

Reporting the winning p-value after many seeds, splits or metrics. In the ISLP Fund lab the best-versus-worst managers, picked after looking, give \(p = 0.038\); Tukey's method over the implied 10 comparisons raises it to 0.186.

selfTest.q: Two models share the test set. Why must the bootstrap indices be identical for both?
selfTest.a: Scores on the same items correlate through item difficulty. Identical indices keep the pairing, so shared difficulty cancels in the difference; independent streams add it as noise.

selfTest.q: Which permutation_type tests a paired accuracy difference, and what does it shuffle?
selfTest.a: 'samples': within each pair it swaps the two models' outcomes (sign flips). The null is a zero mean paired difference.

selfTest.q: Your paired interval is [0.030, 0.068] and the permutation \(p\) is 0.0002 from 9999 resamples. What do you report?
selfTest.a: A 3.0-to-6.8 point gain (observed 4.8) separated from zero, the effect size, the count of comparisons that preceded it, and \(p\) below 0.001. With 9999 resamples 0.0002 is the smallest two-sided \(p\) the test can return, so it is a floor, not a measurement.

selfTest.q: After 20 metric looks, one comparison gives \(p = 0.03\). Ship it?
selfTest.a: No. With 20 looks the family-wise error is near 1 minus \(0.97^{20}\) = 0.46. Adjust with Holm or BH, or pre-register the primary comparison, and report the effect size either way.

practice.locator: Reproduce \(\alpha\) SE 0.0912 (B=1000, seed 0) and the OLS bootstrap SEs from The Bootstrap

practice.name: ISLP Ch13 lab: Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg
practice.locator: Reproduce the Bonferroni and Holm verdicts (only Manager One, then One plus Three at FWER 0.05), the Tukey adjustment from 0.038 to 0.186, and the Benjamini-Hochberg rejections on all 2,000 managers

units.stopWhen: Your paired bootstrap and permutation test agree on a model comparison, the interval uses one index stream, and every p-value ships with an effect size and a comparison count.

fit.note: ISLP covers bootstrap SEs and FWER/FDR but not the paired SciPy API, so the SciPy resampling tutorials were adopted for the paired bootstrap and the paired permutation test.

units.title: Learning curves, error taxonomies and slices
outcomes: Read training and validation curves to separate bias (more data will not help) from variance (more data may help).
Build an error taxonomy with slice support counts and refuse conclusions a slice cannot support.
Turn the worst supported slice into a testable hypothesis with a follow-up slice.
units.why: Aggregate scores average away the slice that fails. Curves say whether to buy data; slices say where the model is wrong.

next.note: Explain the worst slice with importance and dependence views.
Test the slice hypothesis with controls.

study.locator: Sections 3.5.1 (validation_curve and ValidationCurveDisplay: high train with low validation means overfit) and 3.5.2 (learning_curve and LearningCurveDisplay: Naive Bayes flat and low versus SVM converging)
study.depth: Skip the scalability example. The digits snippet numbers in Reproduce are your check.

study.title: Slice, error and data-size requirements
study.locator: Milestones B (record predictions and errors per item), C (prescribed ablations and learning/data-size probes) and E (subgroup, time and source slices with paired uncertainty and practical significance)

focus: Both scores low means bias (capacity or features); train high with validation low means variance. Validation above train is rare and usually means the two are measured differently: augmentation or dropout at train time, an easier or tiny validation split, or leakage.
Never tune on the validation curve's peak and report that peak. The curve diagnoses; a fresh split evaluates.
Every slice needs its support count beside the rate: 100% error on \(n=3\) is a hint, not a finding.
Slice by deployment axes (source, time, subgroup), not by the model's own confidence alone, or the taxonomy confirms itself.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run learning_curve for LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000) on digits with train_sizes [0.1, 0.5, 1.0] and cv=3 (119, 599 and 1198 training rows) and read the regime. Reference run: train 1.00 at every size, validation 0.823, 0.918, 0.926, so variance at small \(n\) with a closing gap. Then tabulate one error slice with support counts.
traps: Concluding that more data will fix flat converging curves. The Naive Bayes panel shows both scores stuck low: capacity, not data.
Slicing until a bad slice appears, then reporting it raw. Unplanned slices are multiple comparisons, so pre-register slices or adjust.
Averaging slice metrics without support weights while claiming deployment impact. Impact is rate times slice share.

selfTest.q: Train 1.00 with validation 0.82 at small \(n\), then 1.00 with 0.93 at full \(n\). Diagnosis?
selfTest.a: Variance-dominated with a closing gap: more data helped and the model still memorizes train. Some overfit remains, so try regularization, not just data.

selfTest.q: Both curves sit flat at 0.70 from 10% to 100% of data. Next step?
selfTest.a: Bias: capacity or features are the ceiling. More of the same data will not move it, so change the model or the representation.

selfTest.q: Slice A is 2/3 wrong. Slice B is 40/400 wrong. Which finding is stronger?
selfTest.a: B: 10% error on \(n=400\) has a tight interval, while 67% on \(n=3\) is noise. Report both with counts and intervals.

selfTest.q: Why slice by source or time rather than by low model confidence?
selfTest.a: Confidence slices re-select the model's own failures and cannot show where deployment breaks. Source and time slices test the deployment axes.

practice.name: scikit-learn learning-curve digits check
practice.locator: Reproduce the Naive Bayes versus SVC learning-curve comparison on digits and state the bias or variance reading for each panel
practice.note: Match the qualitative pattern (flat low Naive Bayes, converging SVM), not pixel values. Then repeat on your own data with support-counted slices.

units.stopWhen: Your curve reading names bias or variance with the numbers that show it, and every slice claim carries \(n\) and an interval.

fit.note: Curves come from the sklearn route and slices with data-size probes from the investigation spec; nothing missing.

units.title: Permutation importance and partial dependence
outcomes: Compute permutation importance on a held-out set with repeats and report importances with their spread.
Distrust importance and PDP readings under correlated features and check with clustered or ICE views.
State PDP and ICE results as model behavior on constructed points, never as causal effects.
units.why: Importance and dependence plots describe what the fitted model leans on, not what causes the outcome. Correlated features make both lie smoothly.

next.note: Test an important feature by removing it under controls.
Correlated structure is what shift breaks first.

study.title: Permutation feature importance
study.locator: The diabetes Ridge worked example (s5 0.204, bmi 0.176, bp 0.088, sex 0.056 at n_repeats=30), Section 5.2.2 (impurity/MDI bias toward high-cardinality features) and Section 5.2.3 (correlated features share credit; cluster and keep one per group)
study.depth: Skip the multicollinear example figures. The breast-cancer warning paragraph carries the point.

study.title: Partial dependence and ICE plots
study.locator: Section 5.1 (PDP marginalizes over complement features; correlated inputs create absurd constructed points), Section 5.1.2 (ICE lines with kind='both' reveal hidden heterogeneity) and Section 5.1.4 (brute versus recursion can disagree under correlation)
study.depth: Stop before the multi-class dropdown. One binary or regression example is enough.

focus: Permutation importance is model- and score-relative: shuffle one column, measure the score drop, repeat. Importance is the reference minus the corrupted mean.
Compute it on held-out data with a decent model. On a bad model low importance means nothing; train versus held-out gaps flag overfit.
Under correlation, permutation importance splits credit across partners and PDP averages over impossible combinations. Cluster correlated features first and overlay ICE.
Impurity (MDI) importance favors high-cardinality and numeric features and rewards overfit. Never present it as interchangeable with permutation importance.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run the diabetes Ridge permutation snippet (n_repeats=30, random_state=0) and recover the top-4 order with s5 near 0.204. Then plot centered ICE lines for bmi: Ridge is linear, so every line is identical. Refit HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0) on the same split and its centered ICE lines end anywhere from about 36 to 152; describe where they spread.
traps: Dropping unimportant correlated features one at a time. Partners cover for each other, so remove the cluster or nothing.
Reading a PDP slope as raising \(X\) raises \(Y\). PDP shows model output on constructed rows with complement values borrowed from other rows; no intervention happened.
Quoting MDI importances as feature truth. They are computed on training splits during fitting and biased toward fine-grained splitters.

selfTest.q: Permutation importance of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) (correlation 0.95) is near zero for both, yet dropping both tanks the score. Explain.
selfTest.a: The fitted model reads the same signal through both columns, so shuffling one leaves the partner carrying most of it and each drop looks small. Removing both removes the signal. Cluster correlated features and judge the cluster.

selfTest.q: Why must permutation importance run on a held-out set with a decent model?
selfTest.a: On training data it measures memorization leverage, and on a bad model the reference score is meaningless. Held-out drops measure reliance that generalizes.

selfTest.q: The temperature PDP falls above 35C but some ICE lines are flat. What do you conclude?
selfTest.a: The average hides heterogeneity: heat hurts only a subgroup, an interaction. Report the ICE spread, not just the PD line.

selfTest.q: MDI ranks a 1000-level id column first while permutation ranks it near zero with large spread. Which do you trust?
selfTest.a: Permutation on held-out data. MDI is biased to high-cardinality splitters and computed in-sample: the id memorizes but does not generalize.

practice.name: scikit-learn permutation importance titanic check
practice.locator: Reproduce the RandomForest titanic result: random_cat and random_num sit near zero importance while real features stand out, with spread over repeats
practice.note: Then repeat the diabetes snippet locally and confirm s5 at 0.204 +/- 0.050 before trusting your own run.

units.stopWhen: Your permutation ranking matches the docs' diabetes order, and you can show one correlated-feature trap and one PDP-heterogeneity trap on your own model.

fit.note: Permutation importance is a named stop in the section pool; PDP comes from the same sklearn docs family (Inspection chapter), verified page for page.

units.title: Covariate, label and concept shift, drift and label delay
outcomes: Classify a change as covariate, label or concept shift by naming which distribution moved.
Build a domain-classifier covariate-shift detector and apply importance weights with the support condition checked.
Separate data drift from performance drift and design monitoring that survives label delay.
units.why: Test error assumes tomorrow looks like yesterday. Each shift type breaks a different link, so each needs its own detector and response.

next.note: Prove the shift response with ablations and controls.
Feed drift monitors with audited schema and provenance.

study.title: D2L Section 4.7: shift types and corrections
study.locator: Types (covariate: \(P(y \mid x)\) fixed with \(p(x)\) moved; label: \(P(y)\) moved with \(P(x \mid y)\) fixed; concept: \(P(y \mid x)\) moved), Correction (importance weights \(\beta = p(x)/q(x)\) via a domain classifier, the label-shift confusion-matrix solve) and Taxonomy (batch versus online deployment)
study.depth: Skim the anecdotes and fairness sections. Work the math in Correction.

study.title: D2L 4.7 Exercises: detector and corrector
study.locator: Exercises 2 and 3: implement a covariate shift detector (hint: build a classifier) and a covariate shift corrector

study.title: Shift probes, label delay and monitoring design
study.locator: Milestones C (shift probes) and E (slices with paired uncertainty), failure injection (label delay, shifted prevalence, group overlap) and the monitoring-design stretch goal

focus: Name the moving piece: covariate moves \(p(x)\), label moves \(p(y)\), concept moves \(P(y \mid x)\). The detector and the fix follow the name.

Covariate correction reweights by \(\beta = p_{\text{test}}(x)/p_{\text{train}}(x)\), estimated as \(\exp(h(x))\) from a train-versus-test logistic domain classifier on equal sample counts (otherwise scale by the count ratio), capped as \(\min(\exp(h), c)\). It needs train support everywhere test reaches.
Label shift solves mean-test-predictions equals confusion-matrix times new priors. It needs \(P(x \mid y)\) fixed and a validated confusion matrix.
Data drift without performance drift is a warning, not a failure. With label delay, performance drift stays unobservable until labels land, so monitor input drift and slice volumes meanwhile.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, simulate a covariate shift on a toy problem (train on one \(x\)-range, test shifted), train the domain classifier, compute capped weights \(\beta = \min(\exp(h), c)\), and show the weighted error estimate moving toward the test error.
traps: Correcting with weights where test reaches and train never went. Importance weights cannot invent unseen regions; collect data instead.
Reading a domain-classifier AUC near 0.5 as no shift. It may be a weak detector, so check slice volumes and the performance series too.
Waiting for late labels to detect breakage. Design input-drift and volume monitors that fire before labels land.

selfTest.q: Cat photos train, cartoon cats test. Which shift, and what stays fixed?
selfTest.a: Covariate shift: \(P(y \mid x)\), what makes a cat a cat, is fixed while \(p(x)\) moved. Reweight or adapt features; the labeling rule stands.

selfTest.q: Disease prevalence doubles with identical symptoms per disease. Which shift, and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Label shift: \(P(y)\) moved with \(P(x \mid y)\) fixed. Estimate the new priors with the confusion-matrix solve and reweight by the prior ratio.

selfTest.q: Spammers keep crafting messages unlike anything seen before, month after month. Which kind of shift, and what helps?
selfTest.a: Nonstationary, adversarial drift, D2L's spam example. \(p(x)\) moves into regions training never covered, and where spam imitates normal mail \(P(y \mid x)\) moves too, so it is not a clean covariate shift. Reweighting cannot help without support; relabel recent data and retrain on a schedule.

selfTest.q: Input drift alarms fire but held-out accuracy holds. Ship or stop?
selfTest.a: Neither yet: data drift without performance drift is a warning. Check slice volumes, label-delay horizons and support coverage before changing anything.

practice.name: D2L 4.7 Exercises: shift detector and corrector
practice.locator: Exercises 2 and 3: a domain-classifier covariate-shift detector and an importance-weighted corrector on a controlled synthetic shift
practice.note: Control the shift yourself (one variable moves) so you know the ground truth the detector must find.

units.stopWhen: You classify a new change into covariate, label or concept shift on sight, and your detector plus weighted estimate respond correctly to a synthetic shift you control.

fit.note: D2L covers types, detection and correction; the spec adds shift probes, label-delay injection and monitoring design.

units.title: Ablations, negative controls, threats to validity and decision memos
outcomes: Design the smallest ablation matrix that separates data, feature, capacity and evaluation explanations.
Keep a null control (dummy baseline, shuffled-target run) that must fail for the conclusion to mean anything.
Write a narrow decision memo that survives a small move in the best score.
units.why: A higher score is not evidence until cheaper explanations are ruled out. Ablations and negative controls turn a leaderboard into a finding.

next.note: Give every ablation cell paired uncertainty.
Return stronger baselines as standing controls.

study.title: Ablations, failure injection and defense
study.locator: Milestones C (prescribed ablations under one controlled search budget), D (inject target-proxy, duplicate, future-feature, global-preprocessing and test-tuned-threshold failures; audits must fail at the right boundary; preserve failed runs), E (effects with paired uncertainty and multiplicity) and the Design-defense questions (baseline, metric-threshold match, what each ablation isolated, the largest remaining shift)

study.title: Dummy estimators as null controls
study.locator: Section 3.4.8 (most_frequent, stratified and uniform baselines that ignore the features; the worked example sets the bar the real model must clear)

study.title: Common pitfalls: leakage patterns that audits must catch
study.locator: Section 12.2 (split-first discipline, scaler-in-pipeline, the SelectKBest-on-all-data pattern scoring 0.76 on random labels versus 0.50 split-first)

focus: Change one mechanism per cell with data, splits and evaluation frozen. Record every variant and failure, not just the winner.
Every claim needs a null that must fail: a dummy baseline, a shuffled-target run, or a seeded leak the audit must catch.
Tune all compared families under one controlled search budget. Unequal tuning is a confound, not a result.
Write the memo narrow: decision, evidence, uncertainty, threats, and what would change the call. A conclusion that breaks on a 0.005 score move is not a conclusion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, reproduce the SelectKBest leakage pattern (0.76 leaked on random labels versus 0.50 split-first), then seed one failure of your choice (global scaling before the split) on a small pipeline and show the split-first pipeline removing it beside a dummy baseline.
traps: Ablating by removing a component and retuning everything else freely. Retuning confounds the comparison; freeze the budget and the protocol.
Keeping only the winning run. Without the failed variants and the search history, the winner's curse makes the margin a lie.
A negative control that passes. If the dummy or shuffled-target run looks good, the evaluation is broken, not the model brilliant.

selfTest.q: Removing feature set X drops accuracy 0.02 with a paired interval of [-0.01, 0.05]. What do you conclude?
selfTest.a: Nothing about X yet: the interval covers zero and the effect is noise-sized. Report the null result with its interval instead of claiming X is useless or useful.

selfTest.q: On a balanced binary task, your shuffled-target control scores 0.76. What is broken?
selfTest.a: The evaluation leaks: with random labels nothing beats chance, 0.50 here. Audit preprocessing scope, duplicates and target-derived features before any modeling claim.

selfTest.q: Model A had 3x the tuning budget of model B and wins by 0.01. Decision?
selfTest.a: No decision: tuning effort confounds family quality. Re-run under one controlled budget with paired uncertainty, then decide.

selfTest.q: What makes a decision memo narrow?
selfTest.a: One decision, the exact evidence for it, uncertainty and threats against it, and the pre-stated tripwire (score move, slice failure, shift) that would reverse it.

practice.name: Seeded-leak audit drill (SelectKBest pattern)
practice.locator: Section 12.2.2: reproduce the leaked 0.76 on random labels, then the split-first 0.50, on your own data with one seeded leak of your choice
practice.note: Add a dummy-baseline null control and keep the failed run in your log. That log is the memo's appendix.

units.stopWhen: A seeded leak fails your audit at the right boundary, every ablation cell carries paired uncertainty, and your memo states the tripwire that would reverse the decision.

fit.note: Ablations, failure injection and decision defense come from the investigation spec; dummy nulls and leakage patterns from the sklearn route.
